title: Trapping Rain Water II
summary: Given a matrix heightMap of dimensions m x n, representing the elevation of each cell, calculate the total volume of water that can be trapped after a rainfall.
statement: Given a matrix heightMap of dimensions m x n, representing the elevation of each cell, calculate the total volume of water that can be trapped after a rainfall.
constraints: 1 <= rows, columns <= 200; the matrix is rectangular.
0 <= height_map[r][c] <= 20,000; each cell has unit area.
Water escapes through the boundary along four edge-adjacent directions, not diagonally. Return total volume.
hints: An escape path can wind around obstacles; immediate walls alone do not determine water depth.
Start from every boundary cell and expand from the lowest effective frontier using a min-heap.
Pop level; for each unseen neighbor h add max(0,level-h), mark seen, and push max(level,h).
The lowest frontier fixes the smallest escape level. Carry that effective level, not just the terrain height.
editorial: Flood inward from the exterior through the lowest frontier. Any lower escape route would already have been processed when a new cell is reached, so its surface is max(frontier,terrain). Add the difference and propagate the effective surface. Seed each boundary once. The iterative flood practices connected-region reasoning without overflowing Python recursion on 40,000 cells.

tests.explanation: Interior cells at row 1, columns 1, 2, and 4 (zero-based) hold 1, 2, and 1 units: total 4.
The zero-height gap in the left boundary connects all interior zeros to the outside, so no water remains.
